title: Sources & Methodology
text:
This study examines the relationship between tourism, accommodation capacity, employment, and economic activity in the U.S. Virgin Islands from 2000 through 2025. It uses descriptive time-series analysis and cross-source comparisons to assess the scale and unevenness of the territory’s tourism recovery following Hurricanes Irma and Maria (2017) and the COVID-19 pandemic (2020).
The analysis combines visitor statistics, accommodation surveys, federal employment and economic data, business census snapshots, and National Park Service visitation records. These sources measure different aspects of the tourism economy and are not treated as interchangeable.
The study is descriptive. It identifies changes and divergences across indicators but does not estimate the independent causal effects of hurricanes, the pandemic, or federal recovery spending.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Data Acquisition and Preparation
Original source files are retained in data/raw/. Source metadata, including URLs, local paths, coverage, frequency, and known limitations, are maintained in src/acquisition.py. Processing and loading functions are maintained in src/cleaning.py; chart construction is centralized in src/charts.py.
Manually extracted hotel statistics from USVIBER reports are stored as separate annual source files and combined by src/hotel_extraction.py. The extraction process checks for duplicate years, merges available, occupied, and occupancy series by year, and calculates an independent occupancy rate:
\[
\text{Calculated occupancy} =
\frac{\text{Room nights occupied}}{\text{Room nights available}}
\times 100
\]
The calculated rate is retained alongside the published occupancy series rather than assumed to be equivalent to it.
Census data are assembled from the 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2022 Economic Census releases. Overlapping observations are deduplicated by year and industry. Where vintages overlap, the earlier vintage is retained in the employment analysis.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Tourism Arrivals
Visitor statistics are drawn primarily from USVIBER Annual Tourism Indicators. The analysis uses published annual totals for total visitors, air visitors, and cruise passengers. These measures are retained as reported rather than reconstructed from visitor-type components, which do not consistently sum to published totals.
Historical coverage combines report vintages. TOUR24 supplies 2000 and 2010–2024 observations; TOUR10 supplies 2001–2009, where the later publication does not provide a consistent historical series. The change in source vintage is documented because some historical values were revised. Accommodation-related series are retained separately where their historical coverage is consistent across publications.
The analysis does not use the overnight-tourist series. Air visitors and cruise passengers are treated as separate published arrival measures, not as proxies for overnight stays or total visitor spending. The World Bank’s 2020 international-arrivals observation is excluded as an implausible outlier during the pandemic-related shutdown of cruise tourism.
Visitor counts represent arrivals, not unique individuals. They do not measure length of stay, visitor-days, or economic contribution. Comparisons with accommodation, employment, and economic indicators therefore describe related dimensions of the tourism economy rather than a direct accounting relationship.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Employment and Compensation
Three sources provide complementary measures of employment:

FRED Leisure and Hospitality: Monthly seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted employment. Annual values are calculated as the mean of the twelve monthly observations, not their sum. The series covers the broader Leisure and Hospitality sector (NAICS 71 and 72), not tourism alone.
USVIBER tourism employment: Published employment categories for hotels and lodging, and eating and drinking establishments. The available series ends in 2022.
BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW): Annual average employment, wages, and establishments for NAICS 72, 721, and 722. QCEW counts covered jobs rather than unique workers and excludes self-employed and other uncovered workers.

Census employment figures are March pay-period snapshots, not annual averages. Census, QCEW, FRED, and USVIBER employment figures are therefore compared as indicators of related activity, not as equivalent counts.
QCEW average annual pay is calculated as total annual wages divided by annual average employment. Nominal wages and payroll are adjusted to approximate 2016 dollars using the mainland U.S. CPI-U. This is an inflation proxy, not a USVI-specific price adjustment.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Accommodation Capacity and Utilization
Accommodation capacity is measured using two distinct sources:

USVIBER annual tourism indicators: Survey-based counts of hotels, hotel rooms, and condominium or other accommodation units.
Economic Census: Establishments and guestroom counts for payroll-filing accommodation businesses, primarily NAICS 7211.

These sources have different coverage. The USVIBER survey includes a broader range of accommodation providers; Census counts are limited to businesses meeting its reporting criteria. Their totals are not combined.
Historical Census guestroom counts require a crosswalk between table formats. The 2007 and 2012 figures use the A10 industry total; the 2017 and 2022 figures use NAPCS product code 7003825000. The 2017 count is a December 31 observation, after Hurricanes Irma and Maria, and is not a pre-hurricane capacity benchmark.
Occupancy is examined using both USVIBER annual indicators and monthly hotel statistics extracted from USVIBER hotel reports. Published occupancy, calculated room-night occupancy, and broader annual survey occupancy are retained as separate measures because their reporting populations and comparability have not been established as identical.
The ratio of annual overnight arrivals to listed rooms was explored as a contextual measure. It is not treated as occupancy or actual room utilization: it does not account for length of stay, room availability throughout the year, or differences in accommodation type.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Economic Output
Territorial GDP and industry value added are drawn from BEA tables:

Table 1.1: nominal GDP.
Table 1.2: real GDP in chained 2012 dollars.
Table 2.1: nominal industry value added.
Table 2.3: real industry value added in chained dollars.

Real-dollar comparisons use BEA’s chained-dollar measures. No additional CPI adjustment is applied.
Accommodation and food services (A&F) value added is used as an indicator of activity in a relevant part of the visitor economy, not as a measure of tourism GDP. It excludes tourism-related activity in industries such as transportation, retail, and recreation, while including purchases by residents.
A&F’s share of GDP is calculated as nominal A&F value added divided by nominal GDP. This is an approximate industry share, not a complete accounting of tourism’s contribution to the economy.
BEA industry-level data end in 2021; GDP totals extend through 2022.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Recovery Comparisons
To compare indicators measured in different units, selected series are indexed to 2016, the last full year before the 2017 hurricanes:
\[
\text{Index}_t =
\frac{\text{Value}_t}{\text{Value}_{2016}}
\times 100
\]
An index of 100 represents the 2016 level. Values above or below 100 indicate levels higher or lower than that baseline.
Each series is indexed independently. Series without a usable 2016 observation are excluded. Missing observations are retained as missing; they are not interpolated or treated as zero. The resulting indices facilitate comparisons of relative change, not absolute scale.
Occupancy rates are not indexed. Changes are expressed in percentage points relative to the 2016 rate, preserving the distinction between a change in a rate and a proportional change in an underlying quantity.
A separate COVID comparison uses 2019, the last pre-pandemic year, as its baseline. It examines visitor arrivals, air visitors, cruise passengers, hotel rooms, FRED employment, and VIIS visitation.
No composite recovery score is calculated. The analysis compares the trajectories of individual indicators because recovery in visitor volume, accommodation capacity, employment, compensation, and economic output need not proceed at the same rate.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
National Park Visitation
National Park Service visitation data are drawn from the IRMA database for Virgin Islands National Park (VIIS) and Buck Island Reef National Monument (BUIS). Annual and monthly observations are retained separately.
NPS visitation represents estimated recreation visits, not unique visitors. VIIS estimates also involve changes in counting methods over time. The 2003–2021 and 2022–2025 estimates are treated as distinct methodological periods; 2026 observations are excluded from long-term comparisons because of a major change to traffic-counter-based estimation. Missing BUIS observations for 1999–2001 are not interpolated.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Data Quality and Limitations
Source discrepancies and known data-quality issues are documented in src/validation.py. The project maintains a structured data-quality log recording the issue, severity, treatment, and implications for interpretation.
Key decisions include:

Excluding the anomalous 2020 World Bank international-arrivals observation rather than treating it as valid.
Using published USVIBER visitor totals and categories directly rather than reconstructing totals from components that do not consistently reconcile.
Combining historical USVIBER tourism-indicator vintages where necessary, while documenting material differences between publications.
Retaining gaps in NPS and hotel reporting rather than interpolating missing years.
Treating 2025 hotel observations as partial where the source reporting period does not cover a full year.
Using FRED employment after the USVIBER employment series ends in 2022.
Treating mainland CPI-U as an approximate deflator for USVI wages, not a local cost-of-living measure.

The analysis is constrained by differences in source coverage, definitions, reporting frequency, and revision history. Indexed comparisons reduce differences in scale but do not eliminate these limitations. Conclusions are therefore based on converging or diverging indicators, not on any single series.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Reproducibility
The project separates acquisition, validation, cleaning, hotel extraction, and chart construction into modules under src/. Raw source files are retained separately from processed datasets. Processed hotel statistics are generated from the curated extraction files; the analysis loads the resulting annual dataset.
The analysis scripts and source registry document the inputs and transformations used to produce the figures and comparisons. Data-quality decisions are recorded in the validation log.

title: Analysis
text: This report follows one analytical question through the principal evidence: did the USVI tourism economy return to its former scale after 2017 and 2020, or did it return to visitor activity on a smaller operational base? It distinguishes sources and reference periods rather than forcing them into a single composite result.

title: Analysis
text:
Analytical question
How did the scale and composition of visitor arrivals change across the 2017 and 2020 shocks? The answer requires keeping published arrival measures separate.




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Published total, air, and cruise arrivals, 2000–2024. Total visitors is a published aggregate; it should not be reconstructed from the air and cruise series.




Total arrivals fell from 2.585 million in 2016 to 2.143 million in 2018, or 83% of the 2016 level. The 2020 low was not the same as the hurricane interruption: COVID closed cruise shipping and sharply restricted air travel. In 2024, air arrivals were 884,200, 109% of their 2016 level, and cruise passengers were 1.600 million, 90%. The published total was 2.507 million, 97%.
The 2019-2020 comparison clarifies the character of the pandemic. Air visitors fell from 653,700 to 206,300, while cruise passengers fell from 1.433 million to 358,900. Both measures rebounded, but cruise traffic remained structurally weaker after 2020.




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Total visitor expenditure in nominal dollars and approximate 2016 dollars. The real series uses mainland CPI-U, not a USVI-specific cost-of-living index.




Nominal expenditure recovered to $1.829 billion in 2024, 98% of its 2016 value. In approximate 2016 dollars, it was $1.399 billion, 75% of 2016. That real comparison should be read with care: mainland CPI-U is only a proxy, and USVI expenditure may contain substantial changes in trip composition that a deflator cannot isolate.
There is no defensible category-level expenditure breakdown in the available data. The report therefore uses total visitor expenditure only.

title: Analysis
text:
Analytical question
Did hotel capacity return as visitor traffic did, and what does reported occupancy establish?




                            
                                            


Figure 3: USVIBER hotel-room survey inventory and Census accommodation guestrooms. The two series represent different populations and should not be combined.




USVIBER hotel rooms fell from 3,819 in 2016 to 3,127 in 2024, 82% of the earlier level. Census guestroom counts fell from 5,027 in 2012 to 2,039 in 2022. The vintages use different guestroom definitions, and the 2017 count is a December 31 post-hurricane snapshot. It is not a pre-hurricane baseline.




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Published annual occupancy and room-night occupancy rates. 2025 room-night observations are partial or unavailable and are not used for full-year comparison.




Published occupancy reached 66.3% in 2024, from 56.7% in 2016: a 9.6 percentage-point increase. The published 2024 rate is not identical to the separately calculated 60.3% ratio of occupied and available room-nights. They share the direction but should remain separate measures.
Higher utilization can be consistent with a smaller inventory. It does not establish whether occupied room-nights, revenue, or profitability recovered.

title: Analysis
text:
Analytical question
Which employment measures support a labor-market recovery claim, and which are too different to compare directly?




                            
                                            


Figure 5: FRED/BLS Leisure and Hospitality employment, 2000–2025. Values are seasonally adjusted monthly observations, summarized here as annual means.




The FRED series covers broad NAICS 71+72, not tourism employment alone. Its 2024 annual mean was 6.98 thousand employees, 91% of the 2016 mean. The 2025 mean was 6.49 thousand, 84%. This is a decline in the broad sector from 2024, even though 2024 visitor arrivals were near 2016.




                            
                                            


Figure 6: Related employment measures at their source values. Coverage and reference periods differ: annual averages, March Census snapshots, and USVIBER categories.




QCEW employment fell from 6,775 annual average jobs in 2016 to 3,826 in 2020 and was 6,275 in 2025. It is UI-covered employment, not a count of people. Average annual pay is total wages divided by annual average employment, not typical individual earnings.
The Census Economic Census provides only 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2022 snapshots. Accommodation employment was 3,876 in 2012 and 1,650 in 2022. It cannot be treated as an annual series or directly combined with QCEW or FRED.

title: Analysis
text:
Analytical question
What can BEA GDP and value-added data establish about tourism, and what is outside their scope?




                            
                                            


Figure 7: BEA real USVI GDP and real Accommodation and Food Services value added, each indexed to 2016 = 100. BEA series are already real chained-dollar measures.




Real GDP rose from 100 in 2016 to 119 in 2022. The latest BEA GDP observation is therefore above the hurricane baseline. Accommodation and Food Services real value added remained below 2016: 87 in 2021, the last available industry year.
These are different concepts. Real GDP includes the entire territorial economy. Accommodation and Food Services is a broad industry that includes resident-serving activity and excludes tourism-related activity recorded in transportation, retail, and recreation.




                            
                                            


Figure 8: Accommodation and Food Services nominal value added as an approximate share of nominal GDP, 2002–2021.




The A&F share of nominal GDP fell from 12.7% in 2016 to 11.0% in 2021, with a 6.0% low in 2020. The numerator and denominator are not perfectly equivalent concepts, so this is an approximate industry share, not tourism GDP.
Disaster-recovery funding may help explain GDP movement after 2017, but the BEA series alone does not establish a causal channel or quantify the effect.

title: Analysis
text:
Analytical question
Where do the indicators converge, where do they diverge, and what is defensible to conclude?




                            
                                            


Figure 9: Selected indicators indexed independently to 2016 = 100. A rate is not included. Latest observations differ across series.




The lines separate around two shocks. Visitor modes are the fastest to change in 2020 and the most mixed in 2024. Capacity and broad employment remain lower than before 2017. A&F real value added is lower in the latest available industry observation. Real GDP is higher, but it covers the whole territorial economy and is not a tourism recovery index.
NPS visitation adds a useful but non-equivalent recreation signal. The 2025 value of 471,074 is 115% of 2016, but the series uses estimated recreation visits and changed its counting method in 2022. It is not a count of unique visitors.

The strongest supported conclusion is not that the tourism economy fully recovered or failed to recover. It is that recovery is heterogeneous. Arrivals, particularly air arrivals, have returned more completely than accommodation inventory and broad labor measures. Economic output at the territorial level is above 2016 while the Accommodation and Food Services industry remains below it.
The available data do not establish that the post-2020 economy is structurally permanent, nor can they identify the causal share of hurricanes, pandemic losses, federal recovery spending, or changes in visitor behavior. They do establish that 2016 is no longer a uniform benchmark for every dimension of the USVI economy.

title: Trade Winds & Headwinds
text:
The U.S. Virgin Islands’ tourism economy returned through two catastrophic shocks: Hurricanes Irma and Maria in September 2017, and the COVID-19 shutdown of 2020. The first destroyed infrastructure as well as demand. The second interrupted travel again before the islands had recovered.
The useful question is not simply whether tourism is back. It is whether the economy that has reappeared is the same economy that existed before the storms.
The evidence produces a mixed answer. In 2024, published arrivals were close to the 2016 benchmark. Air arrivals exceeded it. Cruise traffic did not. Hotel rooms remained smaller, published occupancy was higher, and broad Leisure and Hospitality employment was still below its former annual average. By 2021, the latest available year for BEA accommodation and food-services value added, that industry remained below its 2016 real-dollar level as well.
Arrivals, capacity, labor, and economic output are therefore not telling the same recovery story. They show a sector that has regained a substantial flow of visitors, but has not restored its full pre-hurricane scale.

title: Trade Winds & Headwinds
section: Two shocks, two kinds of disruption
text:
Two shocks, two kinds of disruption




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Published visitor arrivals by travel mode, 2000–2024. Air visitors and cruise passengers are distinct measures and are not components that should be assumed to sum to total visitors.




The 2017 hurricanes struck in September, when much of that year’s visitation had already occurred. Their full consequences became visible in 2018. Total arrivals fell to about 86% of their 2016 level in 2018 and reached their low point in 2020.
The pandemic altered the mix. In 2020, cruise passengers fell to 25% of their 2019 level, while air visitors fell to 32%. Both have since returned, but at different speeds. By 2024, air visitors reached 109% of the 2016 level, while cruise passengers reached 90%. The published total, which includes the two published modes, stood at 97%.
These are arrivals, not visitor-days. They do not establish length of stay, number of repeat trips, or total spending.

title: Trade Winds & Headwinds
section: A smaller economy serving a large flow of visitors
text:
A smaller economy serving a large flow of visitors




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Selected recovery indicators indexed independently to 2016 = 100. Occupancy is not indexed. Measures have different latest years and source populations.




The visitor base is the clearest partial recovery. Capacity is not.
USVIBER’s reported hotel-room inventory stood at 3,127 rooms in 2024, 82% of the 2016 level. The Census series points to an even sharper change in one payroll-filing population: 2,039 accommodation guest rooms in 2022, down from 5,027 in 2012. Because the Census counts a different population and changed its guestroom product crosswalk in 2017, these numbers should not be combined; together, however, they describe a capacity constraint.
The result is a high published occupancy rate on a smaller inventory. USVIBER reports 66.3% occupancy in 2024, up 9.6 percentage points from 56.7% in 2016. The ratio does not mean the accommodation sector produced 66.3% of prior room nights. It means the remaining inventory was used more intensively.
FRED’s Leisure and Hospitality series broadens the labor view beyond tourism alone. It includes arts, entertainment, and accommodation and food services. Its annual average reached 91% of the 2016 level in 2024 and fell to 84% in 2025. That is a broad labor signal, not a count of tourism jobs.

title: Trade Winds & Headwinds
section: Spending and economic output add context, not a definitive accounting
text:
Spending and economic output add context, not a definitive accounting




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Nominal and approximately 2016-dollar total visitor expenditure (left) and real accommodation and food-services value added (right). The CPI-adjusted expenditure series uses a mainland CPI-U proxy; BEA value added is already chained-dollar real output.




This chart deliberately does not resolve spending and industry output onto a common unit. Nominal expenditure in millions of dollars, approximate real expenditure, and an indexed BEA series answer different questions. It is useful only as a reminder that the available economic measures did not move as neatly as arrivals.
Nominal visitor expenditure reached $1.829 billion in 2024, close to the $1.873 billion recorded in 2016. After converting it with annual mainland CPI-U, however, it was about $1.399 billion in approximate 2016 dollars. The adjustment is not a USVI cost-of-living estimate.
BEA real Accommodation and Food Services value added reached 87% of its 2016 level in 2021, the latest industry observation. This industry is broader than tourism: it includes resident-serving activity, while visitor-related activity in transportation, retail, and recreation appears elsewhere. The series cannot establish tourism GDP or isolate the effect of disaster spending. But it does fit the broader pattern of industry recovery lagging visitor arrivals.

title: Trade Winds & Headwinds
section: What did not recover in the same way

title: Trade Winds & Headwinds
text:
The strongest interpretation
The USVI appears to have recovered much of its visitor flow, but not necessarily the full scale or structure of the tourism economy that existed in 2016. The evidence is consistent with a smaller accommodation stock operating with higher occupancy, uneven labor recovery, and visitor activity that does not map cleanly onto park or industry output.
That conclusion is not a claim that the economy has been permanently transformed. Later observations, especially for 2025 and beyond, may revise the picture. It is a statement about what can be established now: the two major shocks did not leave all indicators at the same stage of recovery.
The next report examines the evidence source by source, and separates visitor counts, room capacity, employment definitions, output measures, and the methodological limits that determine what each comparison can support.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
This study draws on tourism, employment, accommodation, economic, and national park records to examine change in the U.S. Virgin Islands from 2000 through 2025. Sources differ in coverage, frequency, definitions, and reporting practices; the measures are not always directly comparable.
Raw source files are stored in data/raw/. Source URLs, local file paths, coverage, and acquisition notes are catalogued in src/acquisition.py. Validation findings and documented data-quality decisions are maintained in src/validation.py.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Source-specific qualifications
Visitor statistics. USVIBER publications do not always report internally consistent totals. Published total visitors, excursionists, and air visitors are retained as separate measures rather than reconstructed from components that do not reliably sum to the published totals. Historical reports also revise some earlier years. The analysis uses a documented combination of report vintages; figures near the transition between vintages should be interpreted with care.
Accommodation data. USVIBER inventory surveys include a broader range of accommodation providers than Census payroll-based establishment counts. These are different measures, not competing estimates of an identical population. Census guestroom counts also require a classification crosswalk: the 2007 and 2012 figures use the A10 industry total, while the 2017 and 2022 figures use NAPCS product code 7003825000. The 2017 count is a December 31 snapshot, after Hurricanes Irma and Maria.
The hotel-report extraction contains 396 source observations from 66 PDFs. The selected annual series is retained separately from the source observations and conflict log. Available room nights begin in 2007; occupied room nights are missing for 2002; reported occupancy is missing for 2003 and 2018. The 2025 occupied-night and occupancy figures cover only part of the year.
Employment. The employment sources describe different populations and reference periods. FRED Leisure and Hospitality includes Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation as well as Accommodation and Food Services. QCEW covers UI-reported jobs in specified industries. Census employment is a March snapshot, while USVIBER tourism employment uses its own category definitions. These series provide context for one another but should not be treated as interchangeable.
Prices and compensation. Mainland CPI-U is used as a proxy to express QCEW wage measures in approximate 2016 dollars. It is not a USVI-specific cost-of-living measure. The available USVI CPI series ends in 2021 and contains a substantial 2018 discontinuity that has not been resolved; it is therefore not used as the deflator.
Economic output. BEA GDP and industry value added have different end years. Accommodation and Food Services value added includes activity beyond visitor spending and excludes tourism-related activity recorded in other industries. Its share of GDP is therefore an approximate measure of the industry’s contribution, not a tourism-GDP estimate.
National park visitation. VIIS visitation estimates from 2003–2021 and 2022–2025 were produced under different counting methods. The later series is treated as a distinct methodological period. Data from 2026 are excluded because the park shifted to a different traffic-counter-based approach. Park visits should not be interpreted as a count of individual visitors.

title: Data Dictionary

Data availability and reproducibility
The project preserves source files separately from derived datasets. Acquisition metadata are recorded in src/acquisition.py; data loading and preparation are handled in src/cleaning.py. Hotel-report observations, selected values, and conflicts are retained in separate extraction outputs so that the annual series can be traced back to the underlying reports.
Missing observations are not interpolated. Partial-year figures, changes in source definitions, and unresolved discrepancies are identified rather than silently treated as continuous annual measurements.
